title: Three races in the shipped firmware
hints: Each function's read and write sit on either side of `interrupt_window()`, and that's the race. Put the *whole* read…window…write sequence inside one critical section, `__disable_irq()` … `__enable_irq()`. The interrupt isn't lost: it's held pending and runs when you re-enable.

Two tests go further. One checks that interrupts are back **on** afterwards. The other calls your functions while the caller has already disabled interrupts, and checks that they're still **off** afterwards. Write a pair of helpers: `static bool irq_save(void) { bool was = dts_irq_enabled(); __disable_irq(); return was; }` and `static void irq_restore(bool was) { if (was) __enable_irq(); }`.

`uint64_t uptime_ticks(void) { bool s = irq_save(); uint32_t lo = ticks_lo; interrupt_window(); uint32_t hi = ticks_hi; irq_restore(s); return ((uint64_t)hi << 32) | lo; }`. Use the same shape in `events_take` (around `ev = pending_events; window; pending_events = 0;`) and in `events_clear` (around the read, window and masked write). Keep the critical sections that small, with nothing else inside.
